::: {.page-intro}
# BioLIBS

An **Université Grenoble Alpes platform** for multi-elemental imaging of biological tissues by laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS), with the instrument installed at **Grenoble Alpes University Hospital** and connected to pathology and clinical research.
:::

## Multi-elemental imaging of human tissues

BioLIBS is a **Université Grenoble Alpes platform** embedded in the Grenoble academic and hospital ecosystem, with the LIBS instrument physically installed at **CHU Grenoble Alpes** and scientific integration through the **Institute for Advanced Biosciences (IAB — UGA / Inserm / CNRS)**. The platform was inaugurated at CHU Grenoble Alpes in December 2025.

LIBS uses a focused laser pulse to ablate a microscopic amount of material and records the optical emission of the resulting plasma. Repeating this measurement across a tissue section produces spatial maps of multiple chemical elements.

The central question is simple: **what elements are present, where are they located, and what might their distribution mean biologically or clinically?**

## Capabilities

:::: {.grid .research-grid}
::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-4 .research-card}
### Multi-element detection

Simultaneous detection of many elements from the same tissue section, including endogenous elements and exogenous metals or mineral-associated signatures.
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-4 .research-card}
### Spatial imaging

Elemental information is preserved in its histological context, allowing direct comparison with tissue architecture, pathology and adjacent stained sections.
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-4 .research-card}
### High-throughput acquisition

Automated raster imaging enables large numbers of spectra to be acquired across clinically relevant tissue areas, followed by computational processing and elemental image reconstruction.
:::
::::

## Samples & workflow

BioLIBS workflows are being developed for both **formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE)** and **frozen** biological specimens. Depending on the project, elemental maps can be compared with histology, electron microscopy, Raman or FTIR spectroscopy, X-ray fluorescence or other analytical techniques.

::: {.research-strip}
### Typical workflow

**Clinical or biological question → sample selection → tissue sectioning → LIBS acquisition → elemental image reconstruction → pathological / analytical correlation → interpretation**
:::

A major methodological focus is the development of robust calibration, quality-control and quantification strategies suitable for biomedical tissue imaging.

## Applications

:::: {.grid .research-grid}
::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6 .research-card}
### Environmental & occupational exposure

Mapping exogenous elements and mineral-associated signatures in lung and other tissues to investigate past exposure and its possible relationship with disease.
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6 .research-card}
### Respiratory disease

Elemental imaging in interstitial lung disease, sarcoidosis, granulomatous disease and other pulmonary conditions where tissue deposits or exposure history may be informative.
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6 .research-card}
### Cancer & nanomedicine

Tracking metal-containing probes, nanoparticles or elemental signatures in preclinical and clinical oncology research.
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6 .research-card}
### Biomaterials & implants

Characterizing the spatial distribution of metals released from implants or biomaterials and their relationship with surrounding tissue.
:::
::::

## From analytical signal to elemental pathology

The long-term objective is not simply to detect elements, but to establish **elemental pathology** as a spatially resolved complement to conventional tissue analysis: an approach in which chemical composition is interpreted together with morphology, exposure history and clinical context.

This requires validation at every step — sample preparation, acquisition, calibration, image processing, pathological correlation and clinical interpretation.

## Clinical & collaborative research

BioLIBS supports collaborative projects involving pathology, pulmonology, occupational medicine, oncology, toxicology, biomaterials and environmental health. Several clinical and translational programmes use the platform to evaluate where elemental information can add meaningful evidence to established diagnostic and research methods.
